english: I'd like a transit card, please
usage: Polite; said at a convenience store counter buying a T-money card
Add 하나 to specify a single card — natural when there are multiple buyers
Asking by brand name; 티머니 is the dominant card brand in Seoul
Where do I buy a transit card?
Ask this at a hotel or on the street if you can't find a 편의점
examples: 교통카드 주세요.
A transit card, please.
Said to a clerk at a GS25 or CU convenience store counter; hand over cash and the card will be activated for you.
저기요, 티머니 카드 하나 주세요.
Excuse me, one T-money card, please.
Using the brand name 티머니 is completely natural; clerks know it instantly and it is the most common card in Seoul.
A: 교통카드 사려고 하는데 여기서 팔아요? / B: 네, 얼마짜리로 드릴까요?
A: I want to buy a transit card — do you sell them here? / B: Yes, which denomination would you like?
사려고 하다 ('intending to buy') politely checks availability before asking the clerk to retrieve one.
nuance: 교통카드 is 교통 (交通, 'transportation') + 카드 ('card'), the generic umbrella term for the rechargeable tap-to-ride card used on every Korean city subway and bus. In everyday speech Seoulites usually say the brand name 티머니, and 캐시비 is the other major brand common in other cities, but 교통카드 is the safe neutral term that any clerk anywhere understands. You buy one at any 편의점 (convenience store) for a small fee — the card itself costs money and that fee is not refunded. The critical cultural difference from many other transit systems is that you do NOT buy disposable single-journey paper tickets for daily travel; you load cash onto a reusable card and tap in and out. For English speakers the immediate trap is asking for a 표 ('ticket') at a convenience store — that word means a paper ticket for a one-off journey or intercity bus, and a convenience-store clerk will look confused. Also note that 카드 alone in a retail context usually means a credit or debit card, so always say the full 교통카드 to be unambiguous. Register: 주세요 is the natural polite form with any clerk; you would never use 반말 with a stranger behind a counter.

structuredNuance.t: 교통카드 literally decomposes as '交通 card' — transportation card. The real meaning in daily life is the rechargeable contactless card (T-money / Cashbee) you tap on every subway gate and bus reader. You buy it at a 편의점 and load cash onto it; the card itself is not free.

Say this at any 편의점 (GS25, CU, 7-Eleven, Emart24) counter. 주세요 is the polite default with service workers; never use 반말 (informal) with a clerk you don't know. If you want a specific brand, substitute 티머니 주세요 or 캐시비 주세요.

표 means a paper ticket — for single-journey subway tokens (1회용 교통카드) sold at station machines, or intercity bus tickets. Asking for a 표 at a convenience store to ride the city bus/subway daily is the wrong word. Bare 카드 alone could be a credit card, so always say 교통카드 in full.

The single biggest English-speaker mistake is asking for a 표 ('ticket') expecting to ride the city subway daily. Korea uses a tap card system, not paper tickets for daily commuting. Budget for the card's purchase price (a few thousand won) on top of any initial load.

mistakes: Asking for a 표 (ticket) to ride daily.
표 means a paper ticket used for single-journey tokens or intercity buses — not everyday city transit. For daily tapping on the subway and bus, buy a reusable 교통카드, not a 표.
Saying just 카드 주세요 at a convenience store.
Bare 카드 is ambiguous and typically means a credit/debit card in a shop context. Always say 교통카드 주세요 (or 티머니 주세요) to be clear you want a transit card.
Assuming the card is free or the purchase price is a refundable deposit.

The physical 교통카드 card itself costs money (roughly 2,500–4,000 won) and is not refunded when you're done with it. Only the cash balance you loaded is yours to spend; plan for the card cost when budgeting your first purchase.

english: Please charge (load money on) my card
usage: Please load it / top it up
Polite; hand the card to a convenience-store clerk and say this
Amount comes BEFORE 충전; the most natural word order
Ask this first if you're not sure the shop does T-money charging
How much shall I load for you?
The clerk's standard reply; respond with an amount + 원
examples: 충전해 주세요.
Please top it up.
Said while placing your card flat on the counter; the clerk will ask how much.
만 원만 충전해 주세요.
Just 10,000 won, please.
만 원만 ('only 10,000 won') signals a small, exact top-up; 만 원 is the most common amount people load.
A: 교통카드 충전 돼요? / B: 네, 얼마 드릴까요? / A: 오천 원 충전해 주세요.
A: Can I charge a transit card here? / B: Yes, how much? / A: Load 5,000 won, please.
Confirm the shop does it, then state the amount — the natural two-step for an unfamiliar shop.
nuance: 충전 is Sino-Korean 充電, literally 'fill electricity', but in Korea it has extended to mean loading money onto any prepaid balance — a transit card, a gift card, a phone data plan. When you hand your 교통카드 to a convenience-store clerk and say 충전해 주세요, they place it on a pad, you give them cash, and the amount is added to your card. The critical word order is AMOUNT first: 만 원 충전해 주세요 ('load 10,000 won'), NOT 충전해 주세요 만 원 — tacking the amount at the end sounds out of order. Subway stations also have self-serve 교통카드 충전기 (charging machines) that accept cash and give exact change, so you are not limited to convenience stores. The main difference from similar words: 결제 means 'settling a payment' (paying for something you owe), while 충전 means 'adding balance before you use it' — they go in opposite directions. 환불 ('refund') is getting money back. For English speakers the trap is treating 충전 as a battery-only word — it covers any kind of balance top-up in Korean. Register: 주세요 is correct with a clerk; the clerk addresses you back with the honorific 드릴까요.

structuredNuance.t: 충전(充電) literally means 'fill/charge electricity' but has expanded to cover loading money onto any prepaid balance. For a transit card it means 'add cash to the card so you can ride'. The clerk taps your card on a pad; you hand over cash for the amount you state.

Say this at any 편의점 or subway 충전기 (self-service machine). Always state the amount FIRST: 만 원 충전해 주세요. 주세요 is polite-neutral for clerks; the clerk's honorific response is 얼마 충전해 드릴까요? ('how much shall I load for you?').
충전 = adding balance in advance (top-up). 결제 = settling/paying a charge you incurred. 환불 = getting money back. These three verbs run in opposite directions — don't confuse them.
충전하다 (verb) → 충전해 주세요 (request), 충전할게요 (I'll top it up), 충전 됐어요? (did it load?). The self-service machine is 교통카드 충전기. 충전 잔액 = the loaded balance remaining.
Two traps: (1) thinking 충전 is only for batteries/phones — it fully covers transit-card top-ups; and (2) putting the amount after the verb (충전해 주세요 만 원) — Korean puts the amount BEFORE: 만 원 충전해 주세요.

mistakes: Thinking 충전 only means charging a phone or battery.
충전 also means loading money onto a transit card, prepaid gift card, or phone data plan. 교통카드 충전해 주세요 correctly means 'top up my transit card' — it is the standard verb.
Putting the amount after the verb: 충전해 주세요 만 원.
Korean states the amount first: 만 원 충전해 주세요. Tacking 만 원 on the end sounds awkward; lead with the number + 원.
Confusing 충전 (load money) with 결제 (pay) or 환불 (refund).
결제 is settling a payment you already owe; 환불 is getting money back. 충전 is adding balance before you use it — say 충전해 주세요, not 결제해 주세요, to top up your card.

usage: Polite; asking a clerk or checking the gate reader to know your card balance
Could you check the balance, please?
Asking the clerk to read it on the terminal for you
Reporting the gate beep or reader's 잔액 부족 error message
The everyday casual alternative — warmer and very common in speech
examples: 잔액이 얼마예요?
How much balance is left?
Ask a clerk when you're unsure how much is loaded; they tap the card on the reader and tell you.
저기요, 카드 잔액 좀 확인해 주세요.
Excuse me, could you check my card balance?
확인해 주세요 ('please check') is slightly softer than 얼마예요 and signals you want them to look it up for you.
A: 왜 안 열려요? / B: 아, 잔액 부족이래요. 충전해야겠어요.
A: Why won't it open? / B: Oh, it says low balance. I'd better top up.
Reacting to the gate's 잔액 부족 beep — the immediate fix is to step aside and 충전 before trying again.
nuance: 잔액 is Sino-Korean 殘額 ('remaining amount'), the standard financial noun for the balance left on a card. In the transit context it refers specifically to the cash loaded on your 교통카드. The gate reader always shows the remaining balance after each tap, and the dreaded 잔액 부족 ('insufficient balance') beep plus a red light means you cannot ride — step aside, 충전, and try again. The everyday casual alternative 얼마 남았어요? ('how much is left?') feels warmer and less formal because it avoids the Sino-Korean noun, but both are completely natural. The big particle trap for English speakers: because you are asking 'the balance IS how much?', 잔액 is the grammatical subject and takes 이 — so 잔액이 얼마예요?, NOT 잔액을 얼마예요? (the object marker 을 makes no sense here; you are not doing anything to the balance). Do not confuse 잔액 (money stored on the card) with 거스름돈 (cash change handed back) — they describe entirely different flows of money. Polite -요 is right with any clerk or agent.

structuredNuance.t: 잔액(殘額) literally means 'remaining amount'. For a transit card it is the cash balance you have loaded. The gate reader shows this balance after every tap; 잔액 부족 ('insufficient balance') triggers a beep and a locked gate.
Ask a 편의점 clerk (잔액 좀 확인해 주세요) or use the subway 충전기 machine to check. Polite -요 is correct with staff. The casual 얼마 남았어요? works between friends or with a familiar clerk.

잔액이 얼마예요? is precise and formal (uses the financial Sino-Korean noun). 얼마 남았어요? is warm and colloquial — same question, slightly softer register. Neither is wrong; choose by formality. 자리 없어요 ('no seats') looks similar but is unrelated — don't confuse 잔액 (card balance) with 거스름돈 (cash change).
잔액 조회 (balance inquiry, formal/written). 잔액이 얼마 있어요? (how much balance do you have?). 잔액이 부족해요 (the balance is insufficient). These all share the root 잔액.
Use the subject marker 이, not the object marker 을: 잔액이 얼마예요? You are stating 'the balance is how much?', so mark 잔액 as the subject. 잔액을 얼마예요? is ungrammatical.

mistakes: Using 을/를 instead of 이/가: 잔액을 얼마예요?
얼마예요 needs a subject, not an object. The natural form is 잔액이 얼마예요? — you are asking 'the balance is how much?', so mark 잔액 with the subject particle 이.
Confusing 잔액 (card balance) with 거스름돈 (cash change).
잔액 is the money loaded on your card; 거스름돈 is the physical change handed back when you pay cash. To check your card, ask 잔액이 얼마예요? — 거스름돈 is a different transaction entirely.
Ignoring a 잔액 부족 beep and pushing through the gate again.
잔액 부족 means the card lacks sufficient funds and the gate will not open. Trying again repeatedly will not help. Step aside, find a 편의점 or 충전기, top up the card, then try the gate again.

usage: Polite-neutral; asking which numbered subway line a station is on
Asking for directions to a specific line inside a station
Asking which line to board to reach your destination
Confirming which line you are currently standing at
examples: 강남역은 몇 호선이에요?
Which line is Gangnam Station on?
역 + 은 sets the topic, then ask 몇 호선이에요 — Gangnam is on Line 2 (and the Sinbundang Line).
시청 가려면 몇 호선 타야 돼요?
Which line do I take to get to City Hall?
가려면 ('in order to go to') frames the route question naturally; City Hall Station is on Lines 1 and 2.
A: 여기서 2호선으로 어떻게 가요? / B: 저쪽 계단으로 가시면 돼요.
A: How do I get to Line 2 from here? / B: Just head down those stairs over there.
2호선으로 ('toward/to Line 2') uses the direction particle 로, and the natural reply gives a landmark.
nuance: 호선 is the dedicated counter for numbered subway lines: 호(號) means 'number' and 선(線) means 'line'. The full phrase 몇 호선이에요? means 'what number line is it?' and is used constantly inside stations and when checking directions. The single most important grammar point is number system: line numbers ALWAYS use Sino-Korean numerals (일, 이, 삼, 사…), so Line 2 is 이 호선, NEVER 두 호선. This is the most consistent learner mistake because many other Korean counters take native numbers, but 호선 is Sino-Korean all the way. The direction particle toward a line is -으로/-로: 2호선으로 가요 ('go toward Line 2'). English speakers also reach for 라인 (from 'line') or say 라인 2 — Koreans say 호선 for numbered subway lines without exception; 라인 is not used. Named lines that are not numbered (신분당선, 경의중앙선, 공항철도, 수인분당선) do NOT use 호선 — for those, say the full line name. With strangers and station agents, maintain polite -요 form throughout.

structuredNuance.t: 몇 호선이에요? = 'what number line is it?'. 호(號) = 'number', 선(線) = 'line'. The question asks which numbered Seoul Metro line (1–9 + others) a station sits on.

Ask this to any passerby inside the station or to a station agent. Polite -요 is the right register with strangers; you would not drop to 반말 when asking for directions. Inside the station, follow the color-coded signs — but when confused, this question cuts to the point.

호선 is only for NUMBERED lines (1호선 through 9호선 and the few others with numbers). Named lines like 신분당선, 경의중앙선, or 공항철도 have no 호선 suffix — say their full name. If someone asks 신분당선 몇 호선이에요? that's a non-question; just say 신분당선이에요.
몇 호선이에요? → 몇 호선 타요? (which line do you take?), 몇 호선에서 내려요? (which line do I get off on?), 몇 호선으로 갈아타요? (which line do I transfer to?). Same 호선 counter throughout.
Two pitfalls: (1) using 두 호선 instead of 이 호선 for Line 2 — line numbers are ALWAYS Sino-Korean; and (2) saying 라인 2 (English loanword) — Koreans say 호선, never 라인, for subway lines.

mistakes: Using native numbers: 두 호선 for Line 2.
Line numbers take Sino-Korean numerals: 2호선 = 이 호선, 3호선 = 삼 호선. Never 두 호선 or 세 호선 — this is the single most common subway-number mistake.
Saying 라인 instead of 호선.
Korean subway lines are 호선, not 라인. 'Line 2' is 2호선, never 라인 2. Use 호선 for any numbered line.
Forcing 호선 onto named lines like 신분당선.
Named or lettered lines (신분당선, 경의중앙선, 공항철도, 우이신설선) do not take 호선. Say the full name as-is; reserve 호선 for the numbered lines.

english: Does this go to City Hall Station?
usage: Does this go to City Hall Station?
Polite-neutral; confirming a train or bus destination before boarding
Does this bus go to Gangnam?
Same sentence pattern applied to a bus
Is this subway heading toward Incheon?
방향 ('direction') question — useful when direction matters more than a single stop
To reach City Hall, is this the one to take?
타면 돼요 ('is it okay to board this?') confirms both destination and vehicle
examples: 이거 시청역 가요?
Does this go to City Hall Station?
Quick check to a fellow passenger or driver right before you step on — a simple yes/no answer is all you need.
저기요, 이 버스 서울역 가요?
Excuse me, does this bus go to Seoul Station?
Say this to the bus driver as you approach the door; 저기요 gets attention politely without being pushy.
A: 이 지하철 강남 방향 맞아요? / B: 아니요, 반대예요. 저쪽 타세요.
A: Is this subway going the Gangnam direction? / B: No, it's the opposite. Take that side.
맞아요? ('right?') invites confirmation; the answer 반대예요 ('it's the opposite') tells you immediately to cross the platform.
nuance: 이거 시청역 가요? is 이거 ('this one') + the destination + 가요? ('does it go?') — the fastest possible boarding check. The 가요 is plain intransitive 'go to', and Korean spoken style routinely drops destination particles, so 시청역 가요? is fully natural without -에 or -까지. For buses you simply swap 이거 → 이 버스. The critical subway-specific issue is DIRECTION: every numbered line runs in two opposite directions on the same tracks, so even if you are on the correct 호선, you can board the wrong-direction train and ride away from your stop. That is why the 방향 ('direction') follow-up — 강남 방향이에요? — is so valuable. The verb for 'stop at' is 서다, not 가다: if you want to know whether the train halts at a station, ask 시청역 서요?, not 시청역 가요? ('go' and 'stop' are different). Keep all these questions in polite -요 form with strangers, drivers, and agents; 반말 would be rude.

structuredNuance.t: 이거 시청역 가요? = 'this one — does it go to City Hall Station?'. 이거 = this train/bus; 가요 = goes (intransitive). The destination particle is often dropped in speech. The question is designed to be answered with 네/아니요 instantly.

Ask before boarding to any nearby passenger, the bus driver, or a station agent. Polite -요 is right with all of them; 반말 (informal) would be impolite toward strangers. On the subway platform, aim it at someone waiting or a station worker.

가요? = does it go (toward) that destination? 서요? = does it stop at that station? — two different questions. A train going toward Incheon might not stop at your station if it is an express. For confirming direction without naming a stop, use 방향이에요?: 강남 방향이에요?
이거 시청역 가요? → 이 버스 시청역 가요?, 이 열차 시청역 서요?, 이거 시청 방향이에요? — all the same checking structure with different nouns or verbs swapped in.

English speakers over-build: they add -에 (시청역에 가요?) or rephrase as 가는 거예요? Both are grammatical but stiff for a quick boarding check. The natural spoken shortcut drops the particle: 시청역 가요? Also, the most common real mistake is boarding the right line but the wrong direction — always check 방향 too.

mistakes: Boarding the right line but the wrong direction.
One line runs both ways on the same tracks. Even on the correct 호선, confirm direction: ask 강남 방향이에요? or 이거 시청역 가요? before getting on, or you'll ride away from your stop.
Over-translating 'go to' as 가는 거예요? with extra particles.
The natural spoken question drops particles: 이거 시청역 가요? Adding -에 (시청역에 가요?) is grammatically fine but stiffer for a quick boarding check; the crisp form is best.
Confusing 가요? (does it go) with 서요? (does it stop).

가요 asks the destination or heading; 서요 (from 서다 'to stop') asks whether the train halts at a specific station. For 'does this stop at City Hall?' say 시청역 서요?, not 가요? — an express might 가다 in that direction without 서다 there.

usage: Polite-neutral; asking which stop is yours
Confirming this specific stop is the right one
How many more stops to go?
Asking how far is left, counted by stop number
Please tell me when it's my stop
Asking the driver or a fellow passenger to alert you
examples: 남산 가려면 어디서 내려요?
To get to Namsan, where do I get off?
가려면 ('in order to go to') sets up the get-off question — a complete, polite request for directions.
A: 여기서 내리면 돼요? / B: 아니요, 다음이에요.
A: Should I get off here? / B: No, the next one.
내리면 돼요 ('is it okay to get off here?') gets a direct answer; 다음이에요 ('the next one') tells you to stay on.
기사님, 경복궁 가면 내릴 때 좀 알려 주세요.
Driver, when we reach Gyeongbokgung please let me know when to get off.
기사님 is the respectful address for a bus driver; 알려 주세요 ('please inform me') is the polite favor form of 알리다 ('to notify').
nuance: 어디서 내려요? breaks down as 어디 ('where') + 서 (location-of-action particle) + 내려요 ('get off', from 내리다). The particle 서 is non-negotiable here: because 내리다 ('to get off') is an action that HAPPENS AT a place, it takes the dynamic 에서/서, not the static location marker 에. This means 'getting off here' is 여기서 내려요, never 여기에 내려요. The verb pair to master is 타다 (board / get on) vs 내리다 (get off / alight) — they are opposites and cannot be swapped. On city buses stops are not always announced loudly or at all, so 내릴 때 알려 주세요 to the driver (기사님) or a kind neighbor is genuinely practical. To confirm a specific stop as yours: 여기서 내리면 돼요? The most colloquial variant just before your stop is 내릴게요 — 'I'm getting off!' — said aloud to get people near the door to step aside. Do not confuse 내리다 (exit a vehicle) with 떨어지다 ('to fall/drop') — only 내리다 applies to leaving transit. Keep it polite -요 with strangers and staff.

structuredNuance.t: 어디서 내려요? = 'at where do I get off?' 내리다 = to get off / alight (from a vehicle). 어디서 = 'at where' (어디 + action-location particle 서). The question locates the action of alighting.

Ask any fellow passenger or the bus driver (기사님). Polite -요 is right with all. On a crowded bus near your stop, the shorter 내릴게요 ('I'm getting off!') is more effective than a question — it announces your action and prompts people to make way.

타다 = get on / board; 내리다 = get off / alight — these are the essential pair. Saying 어디서 타요? asks where to BOARD, not where to exit. 떨어지다 means 'to fall or drop' and cannot replace 내리다 for exiting transit.
어디서 내려요? → 여기서 내리면 돼요? (is here where I get off?), 내릴 때 알려 주세요 (tell me when to get off), 내릴게요 (I'm getting off — announcing, not asking). All share the root 내리다.

The particle must be 에서/서 (action at a place), NOT 에 (static location): 여기서 내려요, not 여기에 내려요. English 'at here' maps to 에서 when an action happens there. Using 에 is the single most common grammatical slip.

mistakes: Using 에 instead of 서: 어디에 내려요?
Getting off is an action at a location, so it takes 에서/서: 어디서 내려요?, 여기서 내려요. 어디에 내려요 sounds unnatural because 에 marks static existence, not the place where an action occurs.
Mixing up 타다 (get on) and 내리다 (get off).
타다 = board; 내리다 = alight. Saying 어디서 타요? asks where to BOARD, not where to exit. For getting off, always use 내리다: 어디서 내려요?
Saying 떨어져요? to mean 'get off'.
떨어지다 means 'to fall or drop'. To exit a bus or subway, the verb is 내리다: 여기서 내려요. 떨어져요 would imply you physically fall off the vehicle.

usage: Polite; asking the name of the upcoming subway stop
Use 정류장 for buses instead of 역
이번 역 = the stop arriving right now, vs 다음 = the one after it
Is the next one City Hall, right?
Confirming the next stop by name — 맞아요? invites agreement
examples: 다음 역이 어디예요?
What's the next station?
Ask a fellow passenger when you can't read the announcement board — simple and always understood.
저기요, 다음 정류장이 어디예요?
Excuse me, what's the next bus stop?
On a bus, swap 역 for 정류장 — using 역 on a bus sounds incorrect and may confuse the person you ask.
A: 이번 역이 강남역이에요? / B: 네, 이번이 강남이에요.
A: Is this station Gangnam? / B: Yes, this one is Gangnam.
이번 역 = the stop pulling in NOW; 다음 역 = the one after. Mixing them up makes you get off one stop too early or too late.
nuance: 다음 역이 어디예요? is 다음 ('next') + 역 ('station') + 이 어디예요? ('is where/what?'). A common confusion: 이번 역 is the station arriving AT THIS MOMENT (the subway announcement says 이번 역은… 'this stop is…'), while 다음 역 is the station AFTER THAT — one stop further down the line. Mixing these two makes you get off one stop early or late. The other essential vocab swap is 역 vs 정류장: 역 (驛) is a subway or train station, while a bus stop is a 정류장 (停留場) — you would never call a bus stop a 역. Particle note: you are asking 'the next station is where/what?', so 역 is the grammatical subject and takes 이 (subject marker), not 을 (object marker): 다음 역이 어디예요?, not 다음 역을 어디예요?. 어디예요 literally means 'where is it?' but in this context it naturally means 'which station is it?'. Polite -요 is correct with any nearby stranger or station agent.

structuredNuance.t: 다음 역이 어디예요? = 'the next station — which is it?' 어디예요 ('where is it?') here means 'which station is it?' — Koreans use 어디 both for physical location and for 'which one' when asking about named places.
Ask to any nearby passenger or look at the digital station display. Polite -요 is appropriate with strangers. On a bus, swap 역 for 정류장; never say 역 for a bus stop.

이번 역 = the station you are currently arriving at (used in announcements). 다음 역 = the one after that. Using the wrong one means getting off at the wrong stop. For buses, 역 (subway station) → 정류장 (bus stop). 종점 = the final terminus, distinct from any regular stop.
다음 역 ('next subway station') / 다음 정류장 ('next bus stop') / 이번 역 ('current stop') / 마지막 역 ('last station of the journey'). The pattern [이번 / 다음 / 마지막] + 역/정류장 covers all your positional questions.

Two traps: (1) confusing 이번 역 (arriving now) and 다음 역 (the stop after) — this is the most common error leading to missed stops; and (2) using the object marker 을 instead of subject marker 이: 다음 역이 어디예요?, NOT 다음 역을 어디예요?.

mistakes: Confusing 이번 역 (arriving now) with 다음 역 (the one after).
이번 역 is the stop you are currently pulling into; 다음 역 is the next one after that. Announcements use 이번 역은…. Ask 이번 역이 어디예요? for the current stop, 다음 역이 어디예요? for the following one.
Calling a bus stop a 역.
역 is a subway or rail station. A bus stop is a 정류장. On a bus, ask 다음 정류장이 어디예요? — saying 다음 역 on a bus sounds like you're asking about a train station.
Using 을/를: 다음 역을 어디예요?
어디예요 takes a subject, not an object: 다음 역이 어디예요? You are asking 'the next station is where?', so mark 역 with the subject particle 이, not the object marker 을.

english: Where do I go to transfer?
usage: Where do I go to transfer?
Polite; asking the direction to a transfer point inside a station
Checking whether this station offers a transfer connection
I want to transfer to Line 2
Stating the target line before asking or confirming directions
Asking specifically for the 환승 통로 (connecting corridor inside the station)
examples: 환승하려면 어디로 가요?
Where do I go to transfer?
Ask a station agent or fellow passenger mid-journey; the 로 particle signals you want a direction, not a static location.
여기서 3호선으로 환승하고 싶은데 어디로 가요?
I want to transfer to Line 3 here — which way do I go?
State the target line with -으로, then ask direction; giving the information up front helps the person answer quickly.
A: 버스에서 지하철로 환승하면 할인돼요? / B: 네, 30분 안에 찍으면 할인돼요.
A: If I transfer from bus to subway, is there a discount? / B: Yes, as long as you tap within 30 minutes.
A crucial practical exchange: the 환승 할인 ('transfer discount') depends on tapping the same card within the time window.
nuance: 환승 is Sino-Korean 換乘 ('change-ride'), the formal system word for switching between transit lines or modes. 환승하려면 어디로 가요? uses the grammar -려면 ('if/in order to intend to') + 어디로 ('toward where', with the direction particle 로) + 가요? — 'in order to transfer, which direction do I go?'. The direction particle 로/으로 is essential: you are asking which way to HEAD, so it must be 어디로 가요?, not 어디에 가요? (static destination). The biggest practical fact unique to Korea's transit system: if you tap your same 교통카드 when switching within roughly 30 minutes, you receive a 환승 할인 (transfer discount) and often pay little or nothing extra for the connection — but ONLY if you tap both in and out with the same card; paying cash or changing cards forfeits the discount entirely. The colloquial native-Korean equivalent is 갈아타다 ('change and board'); both 환승하다 and 갈아타다 are correct, with 환승 sounding slightly more official or system-level and 갈아타다 more conversational. Polite -요 for agents and strangers.

structuredNuance.t: 환승(換乘) literally 'change-ride'. In practice it means switching subway lines at an interchange station, or moving from bus to subway (or vice versa). The -려면 structure means 'in order to / if you intend to'.

Ask a station agent or look for 환승 signs inside the station. Polite -요 with anyone you ask. 환승 is also used at bus hubs (환승 센터) where you switch between bus routes — the discount rule applies there too.

환승하다 (Sino-Korean, slightly formal/official) and 갈아타다 (native Korean, colloquial) both mean 'to transfer/change'. In everyday speech 갈아타다 is heard more: 2호선으로 갈아타세요. 환승 appears more in signage, apps, and system announcements. Both are always correct.
환승하다 → 환승해요 (transfer), 환승했어요 (I transferred), 환승 통로 (connecting corridor), 환승 할인 (transfer discount), 환승역 (interchange station). 환승 센터 = bus transfer hub.

The direction particle must be 로/으로: 어디로 가요? (which way do I go?). 어디에 가요? marks a static endpoint, not a direction — it sounds slightly off. Also, many English speakers forget to tap out on the bus before tapping in on the subway, losing the 환승 할인 automatically.

mistakes: Not tapping the card on transfer and losing the discount.
The 환승 할인 only applies if you tap OUT and tap IN with the same 교통카드, within the time limit (roughly 30 minutes). Paying cash or switching to a different card forfeits the free or discounted transfer.
Using 에 instead of 로 for direction: 어디에 가요?
'Where do I go (toward)?' uses the direction particle 로/으로: 어디로 가요? 어디에 가요 marks a static destination and sounds odd when you are asking which way to head inside a busy station.
Thinking only 환승하다 is correct and avoiding 갈아타다.
Both are correct. 갈아타다 ('to change and board') is very natural in colloquial speech: 2호선으로 갈아타요. Do not over-rely on the Sino-Korean 환승 everywhere; 갈아타다 is just as common in conversation.

usage: Polite; confirming this is the correct station to transfer at
반말 — only use this with a close friend you are traveling with
Honorific -셔야 — how station staff or an elder addresses you
Which line do I change to?
Asking which specific line to switch onto — 로/으로 marks the target line
examples: 여기서 갈아타면 돼요?
Do I change here?
Confirming with a passenger at the station before you step off — the -면 돼요? ending asks permission or confirmation of a correct action.
사당역에서 4호선으로 갈아타면 돼요.
You change to Line 4 at Sadang Station.
Giving someone else directions: location + line-with-로 + 갈아타면 돼요 is the full informative sentence.
A: 잠실에서 갈아타야 해요? / B: 네, 거기서 2호선으로 갈아타세요.
A: Do I transfer at Jamsil? / B: Yes, change to Line 2 there.
갈아타야 해요 (question) — 갈아타세요 (polite instruction back) — a real exchange with a helpful local.
nuance: 갈아타다 is a native Korean compound: 갈아 (from 갈다 'to change/replace') + 타다 ('to ride/board'), literally 'change what you ride'. It is the most commonly spoken word for transferring — more colloquial than the Sino-Korean 환승하다, and exactly what you'll hear from locals and helpful strangers. 여기서 갈아타면 돼요? uses the confirmation grammar -면 돼요? ('is it okay if…?'), the standard way to check whether an action is correct. Two particles to get right: the PLACE of transfer takes 에서/서 (여기서, 사당역에서) because the action happens AT that station, and the TARGET LINE takes 로/으로 (4호선으로 갈아타요) because 로 marks the direction or destination you are switching toward. Register: 갈아타면 돼요? (polite -요) for strangers; 갈아타세요 (polite command/suggestion) is what staff give back to you; 갈아타 (반말) only with a friend. An English speaker's typical wrong turn is reaching for 바꾸다 ('to exchange an object') — 기차를 바꿔요 sounds like you want to literally exchange the physical train, which is nonsensical; the correct verb for switching which vehicle you ride is 갈아타다.

structuredNuance.t: 갈아타다 = 갈아 (change) + 타다 (ride) = 'to change what you ride'. 여기서 갈아타면 돼요? = 'is it okay to change (vehicles) here?' — a polite request for confirmation that this station is the right transfer point.
Ask to any fellow passenger before stepping off. Polite -요 is right with strangers. Staff tell you 갈아타세요 (polite command) or 갈아타셔야 해요 (you must transfer — honorific). With a friend: 여기서 갈아타 (반말).

갈아타다 = colloquial, native Korean ('change and board'). 환승하다 = formal, Sino-Korean (official signage, apps). Both mean the same thing; 갈아타다 is heard more in everyday speech, 환승 more on signs. Neither is wrong in conversation.
갈아타다 → 갈아타요 (changes), 갈아타세요 (please change — polite request), 갈아타야 해요 (must change), 갈아탔어요 (I changed). The target line always takes 로/으로: 4호선으로 갈아타세요.

Do not use 바꾸다 ('to exchange an object') for changing vehicles — 기차를 바꿔요 sounds like swapping the physical train. The verb is 갈아타다. Also, the place of transfer takes 에서/서 (action at a location), not 에: 여기서 갈아타요, not 여기에 갈아타요.

mistakes: Using 바꾸다 to mean 'change trains'.
바꾸다 is 'to exchange/replace an object'. Switching which vehicle you ride is 갈아타다: 여기서 갈아타요. 기차를 바꿔요 wrongly sounds like you are trying to swap the physical train for a different one.
Marking the place with 에 instead of 서: 여기에 갈아타요.
Transferring happens AT a station, so use the action-location particle 에서/서: 여기서 갈아타요, 사당역에서 갈아타요. Static 에 is wrong for the place of an action.
Using the wrong particle for the target line: 4호선에 갈아타요.
The line you switch TO takes the direction/target particle 로/으로: 4호선으로 갈아타요 ('change to Line 4'). 4호선에 갈아타요 misuses 에 as though it were a destination marker rather than a direction marker.

english: Did you tap your bus card?
usage: Honorific question (with 시) — how a driver or older passenger addresses you
Polite request — reminding someone to tap at the front
Do I tap when getting off too?
Asking about the tap-out requirement, critical for transfer discounts
Plain statement confirming you have already tapped
examples: A: 카드 찍었어요? / B: 네, 찍었어요.
A: Did you tap? / B: Yes, I tapped.
찍다 is the standard verb; the exchange is quick and natural between any two bus riders.
저기요, 내릴 때도 카드 찍어야 돼요?
Excuse me, do I tap when getting off too?
Tap-out is required on Korean city buses to preserve your 환승 할인 and to be charged the correct distance-based fare.
뒷문으로 내릴 때 단말기에 카드 찍으세요.
Tap your card on the reader at the back door when you get off.
단말기 = card reader/terminal; 뒷문 = back door; this sentence describes exactly what to do.
nuance: The everyday verb for tapping a transit card on a reader is 찍다 — literally 'to stamp, press, or dot'. So 'tap your card' is 카드(를) 찍다 and the reader itself is the 단말기. A slightly different but also acceptable alternative is 대다 ('to touch/put against': 카드를 대다), but 찍다 is what most people say and what drivers use in announcements. Korean city buses require TWO taps: once boarding at the front door and again alighting at the back door — this is the 하차 태그 ('alighting tag'). Skipping the tap-out risks voiding the 환승 할인 (transfer discount) on your next connection and may trigger a penalty fare. The honorific 찍으셨어요? (with 시) is how a driver or an older person politely addresses you; your plain answer is 찍었어요. The verb 찍다 has multiple meanings — 사진을 찍다 is 'take a photo', 찍어 먹다 is 'dip and eat' — but in the bus/subway context it unambiguously means tapping the card. One convenience: the same 교통카드 (T-money or Cashbee) works on both buses and subways; there is no separate 'bus-only card'.

structuredNuance.t: 찍다 literally means 'to stamp/press'. For a transit card it means tapping the card on the reader (단말기). Korean buses require tapping TWICE: at boarding (front door) and at alighting (back door — 하차 태그). Missing the tap-out forfeits your 환승 할인 and may charge a penalty.
찍으셨어요? (with honorific 시) is how a driver or elder asks you. You answer 네, 찍었어요. To ask a fellow passenger: 카드 찍었어요? (plain polite). A reminder to someone else: 카드 찍어 주세요.

대다 ('to touch/place against') is also heard — 카드를 대세요 — and is acceptable but less idiomatic. 누르다 ('to press') is for buttons (the bell 벨), not for card tapping. Don't confuse 찍다 (transit card tap) with 찍다 in other contexts: 사진을 찍다 (take a photo), 도장을 찍다 (stamp a seal).

찍다 → 찍어요 (taps), 찍으세요 (please tap — polite instruction), 찍으셨어요? (did you tap? — honorific), 찍었어요 (I tapped — past). 안 찍으면 ('if you don't tap') + consequence is a common warning structure: 안 찍으면 환승 할인이 안 돼요.

Two traps: (1) forgetting to tap OUT at the back door — the tap-out is not optional on Korean buses, unlike some other transit systems; and (2) reaching for 터치하다 or 누르다 for tapping the card reader — the correct verb is 찍다 (or 대다).

mistakes: Forgetting to tap out (하차 태그) when getting off the bus.
Korean buses require tapping AGAIN at the back-door reader when you exit. Skipping the tap-out voids your 환승 할인 and can trigger a penalty fare on the next ride. Always 내릴 때 카드 찍으세요.
Using a verb other than 찍다/대다 for tapping.
The idiomatic verb is 찍다 (or 대다): 카드 찍으세요. Do not say 누르다 ('press a button') or 터치하다 ('touch') — 찍다 is what Koreans say for tapping the card reader.
Thinking you need a separate 'bus card'.
The same 교통카드 (T-money/Cashbee) works on buses, subways, and most intercity trains. There is no special bus-only card to buy; tap the same card you use on the subway.

english: Can I pay with cash too?
usage: Can I pay with cash too?
Polite; asking the bus driver if cash is accepted alongside card
I don't have a card — does cash work?
Explaining the reason first, then asking — a natural softening sequence
현금으로 ('by cash') + 낼게요 ('I'll pay') — stating your payment method
Critical follow-up: city buses often give no change at all
examples: 현금도 돼요?
Can I pay cash too?
Asked to the driver as you board without a card — a single question that tells the driver everything.
카드가 안 돼서 그러는데, 현금 내도 돼요?
My card isn't working, so — can I pay cash?
안 돼서 그러는데 ('because it's not working, so…') politely explains your situation before asking for an exception.
A: 버스 현금 내면 거스름돈 안 줘요? / B: 네, 거스름돈은 없어요. 딱 맞게 내야 돼요.
A: If I pay cash on the bus, no change is given? / B: That's right, no change. You need to have exact change.
딱 맞게 ('exactly fitting') = exact change; this confirms the practical reality of cash payment on Korean city buses.
nuance: 현금 is Sino-Korean 現金 ('current money' = cash), and 현금도 돼요? = 'does cash work too?' — the particle 도 ('also/too') implies 'in addition to the default payment method (card)', the most natural framing when card is the norm and you are checking the alternative. A major practical trap: on most Korean city buses, paying cash means you drop the exact fare into a cash box and walk on — NO change (거스름돈) is given. Overpaying is lost money. Subway station ticket machines DO give change, but buses generally do not. So 거스름돈 줘요? ('do I get change?') is a smart follow-up before handing in a large bill. The payment-method particle is -으로: 현금으로 낼게요 ('I'll pay by cash'), 카드로 낼게요 ('by card'). English speakers' most common mistake is using 돈 ('money' in general) where they mean 현금 — 돈으로 돼요? is grammatically understandable but vague, because 돈 includes card, bank transfer, and cash; say 현금으로 when you mean physical banknotes and coins. Polite -요 with the driver is always correct.

structuredNuance.t: 현금(現金) = physical cash (banknotes and coins). 현금도 돼요? = 'does cash also work?' The particle 도 ('also') signals that card is the assumed default and you are asking whether cash is accepted as an alternative.

Ask the bus driver (기사님) as you approach the front. Polite -요 is right. On a subway, cash goes into the ticket machine (which gives change), not to a person. On buses, prepare exact change because most drivers and cash boxes give none back.
돈 = money in general (includes card balance, bank transfer, cash). 현금 = physical cash only. When you mean physical banknotes/coins, say 현금, not 돈. 현금으로 낼게요 (pay by cash) vs 카드로 낼게요 (pay by card).
현금도 돼요? → 현금 내도 돼요? (same meaning), 현금으로 낼게요 (I'll pay cash), 거스름돈 있어요? (do you have change? — alternate way to ask). On a bus: 교통카드 없어요, 현금으로 해도 돼요? (I don't have a transit card, can I pay cash?).

Two traps: (1) using 돈 when you mean physical cash — say 현금 for clarity; (2) expecting change on a bus — most Korean city buses give NO 거스름돈 for cash, so prepare exact coins or use a 교통카드 to avoid the problem.

mistakes: Expecting change when paying cash on a city bus.
Korean buses usually give NO 거스름돈 (change) for cash — you pay the exact fare or lose the difference. Prepare exact coins, or better, use a 교통카드. Subway ticket machines do give change.
Using 돈 instead of 현금 for 'cash'.
돈 means money in general (including cards and bank balances). Physical cash specifically is 현금: 현금도 돼요? Say 현금으로 낼게요 ('pay by cash'), not 돈으로.
Mixing up the particle: 현금에 낼게요.
'Pay BY cash' uses the means particle 으로: 현금으로 낼게요, 카드로 낼게요. 현금에 is wrong; 으로 marks the method or instrument of payment.

usage: Polite; asking a passerby for the location of a bus stop
Adding 버스 makes it unambiguous — useful on a busy street
Which numbered bus should I take?
Asking which bus by route number before finding the stop
Do I board at this stop?
Confirming this specific stop is the right one to wait at
examples: 저기요, 버스 정류장이 어디예요?
Excuse me, where's the bus stop?
Asked to a passerby on the street; 저기요 draws attention politely without startling them.
강남역 가는 버스 정류장이 어디예요?
Where's the stop for a bus going to Gangnam Station?
가는 ('that goes') is a relative clause narrowing the stop to buses heading toward Gangnam.
A: 146번은 어느 정류장에서 타요? / B: 저 골목 건너편이에요.
A: Which stop do I catch the 146 at? / B: It's just across that alley over there.
어느 정류장에서 타요 = 'at which stop do I board?'; 건너편 = 'the other side / across'.
nuance: 정류장 is Sino-Korean 停留場 ('stopping-staying place'), the word for a bus stop. This is distinct from 역 (驛), which is a subway or rail station — beginners consistently confuse the two, but using 역 for a bus stop sounds wrong to Koreans. Full form: 버스 정류장 (or 버스 정류소, same meaning). Korean buses are identified by route NUMBER (번호), and you ask which one with 몇 번 버스 — route numbers are read as Sino-Korean figures (146번 = 백사십육 번), not counted items. To say where you board, use the action-location particle 에서: 이 정류장에서 타요 ('I board at this stop'), because boarding is an action happening at a place. A subtle but common English-speaker error is asking 버스 어디예요? ('where is the bus?') when they mean the stop — that question asks for the vehicle's current location, not the designated waiting area; ask 정류장 어디예요? instead. 종점 = the final terminus or last stop on a route, not a regular stop. Polite -요 with any stranger on the street.

structuredNuance.t: 정류장(停留場) = 'stopping-staying place' = bus stop. You find the stop and wait there; the bus number tells you which route. 버스 정류장 is the full form; 정류소 is a synonym used interchangeably.

Ask any passerby on the street. Polite -요 is right with strangers. If you already know the route number, add it: 146번 버스 정류장이 어디예요? — giving the route number helps locals point you to the exact stop, since multiple stops for different routes can be near each other.

역 = subway/train station (never use for a bus stop). 정류장 = bus stop. 종점 = the final terminus of a bus route — on a bus near the end of the line, 종점 is the last stop where everyone must get off. These three words mark distinct concepts.
정류장이 어디예요? → 정류장 어디예요? (particle dropped in casual speech), 이 정류장에서 타면 돼요? (do I board here?), 다음 정류장이 어디예요? (what's the next stop?). The same 정류장 root works across all these questions.
Do not ask 버스 어디예요? — that asks where the physical bus vehicle is, not where the stop is. To find the waiting area say 버스 정류장 어디예요? Also, do not use 역 for a bus stop; 역 is subway/rail only.

mistakes: Calling a bus stop a 역.
역 is a subway or train station. A bus stop is a 정류장 (or 버스 정류장). Ask 정류장이 어디예요? for a bus stop; using 역 here confuses locals.
Asking 버스 어디예요? when you mean the stop.
That question asks where the bus VEHICLE currently is. To find the designated waiting area, ask 정류장이 어디예요? or 버스 정류장 어디예요?
Using native numbers for bus route numbers.
Bus route numbers are Sino-Korean: 146번 = 백사십육 번, 7016번 = 칠천십육 번. Do not say 일곱 번 for route 7 — route numbers are read as written figures, not counted items with native numbers.

usage: Polite; asking frequency/wait time to someone at the stop
More precise: 배차 간격 ('dispatch interval') — the official term used on apps and signs
How long do I have to wait?
Asking the wait time directly in minutes
Asking the exact next arrival — often answered with 몇 분 있어요 ('it's in X minutes')
examples: 이 버스 자주 와요?
Does this bus come often?
Ask to someone already waiting at the stop — they usually know the route well and will give a realistic answer.
146번 배차 간격이 어떻게 돼요?
What's the interval for the 146?
배차 간격 (配車間隔) = the time gap between consecutive buses on the same route; the term used on electronic signs and transit apps.
A: 다음 버스 언제 와요? 앱에는 10분이라는데. / B: 맞아요, 한 10분 돼요.
A: When's the next bus? The app says 10 minutes. / B: That's right, about 10 minutes.
Cross-checking the real-time arrival app with a local; 한 10분 ('about 10 minutes') is the natural approximate answer.
nuance: 이 버스 자주 와요? is 이 버스 ('this bus') + 자주 ('often/frequently') + 와요? ('does it come?') — a warm, casual way to gauge how long your wait might be. The more official register uses 배차 간격 (配車間隔): the set interval between buses on a route, the term found on digital signs and apps. In practice most people check a real-time app (카카오맵, 네이버 지도, 서울 버스 앱) or the electronic display at the stop, but knowing 자주 와요? and 언제 와요? lets you ask a human nearby. An important vocabulary distinction: 자주 is an adverb of FREQUENCY ('often'), whereas 빨리 is an adverb of SPEED ('quickly') — 이 버스 빨리 와요? oddly asks 'does it come fast?' (speed), not 'often'. Equally, 많이 ('a lot, in quantity') answers a different question — 버스 많이 와요? sounds like 'do many buses come?' (count), not 'does it come frequently?'. The natural answer from a local is a minute count: 한 10분마다 와요 ('it comes about every 10 minutes'). Polite -요 with fellow passengers at the stop.

structuredNuance.t: 자주 = 'often/frequently' (adverb of frequency). 이 버스 자주 와요? = 'does this bus come often?'. The answer tells you the approximate wait time. The official term for bus frequency is 배차 간격 — the time gap between buses on a route.

Ask a fellow passenger at the stop. Polite -요 is right. For exact arrival times, the real-time apps (카카오맵, 네이버 지도) and the stop's electronic display are more reliable than asking a person, but knowing the question is useful when your phone battery is dead or signal is poor.

자주 = frequently (how often). 빨리 = quickly (how fast). 많이 = a lot/in quantity (how many). Only 자주 correctly asks frequency: 이 버스 자주 와요?. 빨리 와요? asks if it arrives fast; 많이 와요? asks if many buses come at once.
이 버스 자주 와요? → 배차 간격이 어떻게 돼요? (more formal), 얼마나 기다려야 돼요? (how long do I wait?), 다음 버스 언제 와요? (when is the next one?). All probe the same 'wait time' question from different angles.
Do not use 빨리 (speed) or 많이 (quantity) when you mean 자주 (frequency): 이 버스 자주 와요? is 'does it come often?'. 이 버스 많이 와요? sounds like 'are there lots of buses?' — a different and odd question.

mistakes: Using 빨리 (fast) when you mean 자주 (often).
자주 asks how FREQUENTLY the bus runs; 빨리 asks how FAST it travels. 이 버스 자주 와요? = 'does it come often?'. 이 버스 빨리 와요? = 'does it come quickly?' — a very different and less useful question.
Using 많이 for frequency: 버스 많이 와요?
많이 = 'a lot (in quantity)'. 버스 많이 와요? sounds like 'are many buses coming?' (quantity), not 'does this one come frequently?'. Use 자주 for frequency: 이 버스 자주 와요?
Saying 배차 alone without 간격: 배차가 어때요?
배차 간격 together means 'the gap between buses'. 배차 alone means 'vehicle dispatch' and is incomplete for asking about wait time. Say 배차 간격이 어떻게 돼요? or keep it simple with 이 버스 자주 와요?

usage: Polite; asking the last departure time of the night
언제 ('when') variant — slightly more casual than 몇 시
첫차 ('first vehicle of the day') — the exact opposite of 막차
Has the last one already gone?
Asking if service has ended for the night — 끊기다 = 'to be cut off'
examples: 막차 몇 시예요?
What time's the last train?
Ask a station agent late at night — the simplest, most direct form.
지하철 막차 몇 시예요? 자정 전에 끊겨요?
What time's the last subway? Does it stop before midnight?
끊기다 ('to be cut off') is the idiomatic verb for transit service ending for the night; 자정 = midnight.
A: 막차 놓쳤어요. / B: 그럼 심야버스 타거나 택시 타야 돼요.
A: I missed the last train. / B: Then you'll need to take a night bus or a taxi.
놓치다 = 'to miss/let slip'; 심야버스 = late-night bus route that partially replaces the subway after it stops.
nuance: 막차 is 막 ('last/final', a native Korean prefix marking the end) + 차 ('vehicle/train/bus'), compactly meaning 'the last transit vehicle of the day'. This is a critical survival word in Korea because the Seoul subway typically stops running between 11 PM and 1 AM depending on the line and station — missing the 막차 means an expensive taxi or waiting for the 심야버스 (night bus). Its opposite is 첫차 ('first vehicle of the morning'). The verb for service ending is 끊기다 ('to be cut off/severed'): 막차 끊겼어요? = 'has the last one already gone?'. Note that 끊기다 here is not about a phone call dropping; it is the idiom for transit service stopping for the night. To say you missed it: 막차 놓쳤어요 ('I missed the last train'), using 놓치다 ('to miss/let something slip away'). Why not 마지막 기차? Both are understood, but 막차 is the native compound that everyone uses — it is more compact, more natural, and sounds like a local. Time: hours use NATIVE Korean numbers with 시 (열두 시 = 12 o'clock), while minutes use Sino-Korean with 분 (삼십 분 = 30 minutes) — confusing these is a very common learner error.

structuredNuance.t: 막차 = 막 ('last/final') + 차 ('vehicle') = the last subway or bus of the day. 막차 몇 시예요? = 'what time is the last one?'. It is one of the most practically important words a newcomer can learn.

Ask a station agent, fellow passenger, or the driver late at night. Polite -요 is right. Alternatively, check the transit app or the station schedule board — but knowing the phrase is essential when you can't read the sign.

structuredNuance.e: VS 마지막 기차 / 끊기다 vs 끝나다
structuredNuance.t: 마지막 기차 ('the final train') is understandable but unnatural — locals always say 막차. 끊기다 ('be cut off') is the idiomatic verb for service ending, preferred over 끝나다 ('to finish') in transit contexts: 지하철 끊겼어요? is what Koreans say, not 지하철 끝났어요?
막차 몇 시예요? → 막차 언제예요? (when?), 막차 끊겼어요? (has it ended?), 막차 놓쳤어요 (I missed it). 첫차 몇 시예요? = 'what time is the first one?'. 막차 시간표 = last-train timetable.

Two traps: (1) saying 마지막 기차 instead of 막차 — understandable but unnatural; and (2) mixing up number systems for times: hours with 시 use native numbers (열두 시 = 12:00), but minutes use Sino-Korean (삼십 분 = 30 min). Getting this backwards is very common.

mistakes: Saying 마지막 차/기차 instead of 막차.
마지막 차 is understandable but the compact, idiomatic word is 막차 (and 첫차 for the first). Ask 막차 몇 시예요?, not 마지막 기차 몇 시예요?
Using 끝나다 instead of 끊기다 for service ending.
막차 끊겼어요? is the idiomatic question for 'has service ended for the night?'. 끝나다 ('to finish') sounds odd in this context; 끊기다 ('to be cut off') is the natural word for transit shutting down.
Mixing number systems for time.
Hours with 시 use native Korean numbers (열두 시 = 12:00), but minutes use Sino-Korean (삼십 분 = 30 min). So '12:30' is 열두 시 삼십 분 — do not say 십이 시 for the hour.

usage: Polite; the direct way to ask before sitting down
Asking permission to sit — slightly softer/more deferential
Is there a seat / any space?
Asking whether any open seat is available in the car or area
Checking if the spot is occupied — asks about a person rather than vacancy
examples: 이 자리 비었어요?
Is this seat free?
Ask to the person sitting next to the empty seat before you sit — waiting for their nod or verbal 아니요, 없어요 ('no, no one's there').
A: 여기 사람 있어요? / B: 아니요, 앉으세요.
A: Is anyone here? / B: No, please sit down.
The standard exchange: 앉으세요 ('please sit') is the polite invitation to take the seat.
죄송한데, 여기 노약자석이에요.
Sorry, but this is a priority seat.
노약자석 = priority seating reserved for the elderly, disabled, or pregnant — even an empty one should not be taken by a healthy young person.
nuance: 이 자리 비었어요? is 이 자리 ('this seat') + 비었어요? (past/resultant state of 비다 'to be empty'), literally 'is this seat empty/vacant?'. The related options cover slightly different angles: 여기 사람 있어요? checks whether a PERSON is occupying the spot (often the quickest social probe), while 여기 앉아도 돼요? directly asks PERMISSION (more deferential). All are polite -요; 반말 with a stranger on the subway would be rude. A major cultural point: Korean subway cars have clearly marked 노약자석 (priority seats for the elderly, pregnant, or disabled) at the ends of cars, and 임산부 배려석 (pink seats for pregnant passengers) in the middle — even when these are empty, a young healthy person sitting there will draw disapproval from other passengers. 이 자리 비었어요? does not override that etiquette. Vocabulary note: 비었어요 ('it's empty') and 자리 없어요 ('there are no seats') are nearly OPPOSITE: 이 자리 비었어요 = this specific seat is open; 자리 없어요 = all seats are taken. English speakers often use 자유 ('freedom') to translate 'free/vacant' — 이 자리 자유예요? — but 자유 means 'liberty', not 'available'; the correct word for an empty seat is 비다.

structuredNuance.t: 이 자리 비었어요? = 'is this seat empty?' 비다 = to be empty/vacant (intransitive). The past/resultant form 비었어요 describes the current state of emptiness. A nod or 아니요, 없어요 from the neighbor means 'go ahead'.

Always use polite -요 form with strangers on transit. Never drop to 반말 with someone you don't know. On a quiet car, making eye contact and asking quietly is the norm. If the neighbor is wearing headphones, tap your own ear or point to the seat — they understand.

structuredNuance.e: VS 여기 사람 있어요 / 자리 없어요
structuredNuance.t: 이 자리 비었어요? focuses on the seat's vacancy. 여기 사람 있어요? focuses on whether a person is using it — slightly more natural and direct. 자리 없어요 ('there are no seats') = ALL seats are taken, the opposite situation.
이 자리 비었어요? → 여기 앉아도 돼요? (may I sit?), 여기 사람 있어요? (is anyone here?), 자리 있어요? (any seat available?). All are interchangeable for checking a seat; choose the one that feels most natural.

Do not use 자유 ('freedom') for 'free/vacant' — 이 자리 자유예요? means nothing in Korean. A vacant seat is 비었어요 (empty). Also, 비었어요 (this seat is empty) and 자리 없어요 (all seats are taken) are nearly opposites — do not confuse them.

mistakes: Translating 'free' literally with 자유: 이 자리 자유예요?
자유 means 'freedom/liberty', not 'vacant'. An empty/available seat uses 비다: 이 자리 비었어요? or check the occupant: 여기 사람 있어요?
Sitting in 노약자석 or 임산부 배려석 when able-bodied.

Priority seats (노약자석) and pink pregnant-passenger seats (임산부 배려석) should be left empty for those who need them, even on an otherwise empty train. Sitting there as a healthy young rider draws real and immediate social disapproval.
Confusing 이 자리 비었어요 (this seat is empty) with 자리 없어요 (no seats at all).
비었어요 ('it's empty/free') says THIS SPECIFIC SEAT is open; 자리 없어요 ('there aren't seats') means all seats are full. They describe opposite situations — keep them distinct.

usage: Polite; said when squeezing past people toward the door on a crowded train
The most natural and gentle way to make people step aside briefly
Announcing you need to exit at this stop — triggers people near the door to clear the way
More direct request to clear the way — polite but slightly stronger than 잠깐만요
examples: 저기요, 좀 지나갈게요.
Excuse me, let me through.
Said while moving toward the door on a packed subway — 저기요 gets attention first, then the announcement of your intent.
잠깐만요, 내릴게요!
One sec — I'm getting off!
잠깐만요 + 내릴게요 together part a packed crowd right at your stop; locals respond to 내릴게요 very reliably.
A: 죄송합니다, 좀 지나갈게요. 다음에 내려요. / B: 아, 네. 잠깐만요.
A: Sorry, coming through — I'm getting off next. / B: Oh sure, just a second.
A complete real exchange: apologize, announce your intent, state the reason; the response is immediate.
nuance: 좀 지나갈게요 breaks down as 좀 (softener/politeness particle) + 지나가다 ('to pass by/through') + -ㄹ게요 (first-person polite announcement of an intended action). The -ㄹ게요 ending signals 'I'm going to do X, just so you know' — it is courteous by nature, not a command. On a packed Seoul subway this phrase gets you to the door before your stop. The key verb hierarchy from gentlest to most direct: 잠깐만요 ('just a moment', barely a request) → 좀 지나갈게요 ('I'm going to pass through') → 내릴게요 ('I'm getting off' — most effective near your stop) → 좀 비켜 주세요 ('please move aside' — direct but polite). English speakers commonly reach for 실례합니다 ('pardon the intrusion') — correct in formal settings but stiff and overly ceremonial for a quick train-car squeeze; 잠깐만요 or 내릴게요 is what real people say. Also note: 미안해요 alone is an apology for doing something wrong; it does not signal you need to pass. Pair an apology with the action announcement: 죄송합니다, 좀 지나갈게요. The softener 좀 and the -요 ending are load-bearing — dropping them makes the phrase sound blunter and potentially rude.

structuredNuance.t: 좀 지나갈게요 = 'I'm going to pass through (just so you know)'. 지나가다 = to pass by/through; -ㄹ게요 = polite announcement of intended action; 좀 = softener. The whole phrase is a polite way of saying 'coming through, make way please' without issuing a direct command.

Use on crowded subway cars or buses when you need to reach the door before your stop. Polite -요 is essential; dropping 좀 or -요 makes it sound impolite. 내릴게요 (just 'I'm getting off') is the single most effective phrase to use — people at the door will step aside immediately.

실례합니다 = 'pardon the intrusion' — formal and ceremonial, used when interrupting someone's attention (e.g., asking a question at a counter), not for quickly squeezing past on a subway. 좀 비켜 주세요 ('please move aside') is more direct and appropriate for physical crowd navigation.

좀 지나갈게요 → 죄송합니다, 지나갈게요 (sorry, coming through), 잠깐만요 (just a moment), 내릴게요 (I'm getting off), 죄송합니다, 좀 비켜 주세요 (sorry, please move). The shortest version that works every time: 내릴게요 (said twice if needed).
실례합니다 is the wrong choice for a crowd-squeeze — it is too formal and sounds odd in this context. Also, 미안해요 alone apologizes but does NOT tell people you need to pass; add the action: 죄송합니다, 좀 지나갈게요.

mistakes: Using 실례합니다 to squeeze past on a crowded train.
실례합니다 is formal and suited for interrupting someone to ask a question, not for navigating a packed subway car. Say 잠깐만요 ('one moment') or 좀 지나갈게요 ('coming through') to part the crowd naturally.
Staying silent and physically pushing to the door.
Without a word, pushing past feels rude and you may miss your stop in the commotion. Announcing 잠깐만요! or 내릴게요! signals your need clearly — people will reliably step aside when they hear 내릴게요.
Saying 미안해요 alone when you mean 'excuse me, let me by'.
미안해요 apologizes for a wrong you have done but does not signal you need to pass. To move through a crowd, pair any apology with the action: 죄송합니다, 좀 지나갈게요 — or simply say 잠깐만요 to get people to move.

usage: Polite-neutral; checking if a train skips stops before you board
Is this train express or all-stop?
Asking which type it is directly — useful when signs are unclear
Does the express stop at City Hall?
The critical follow-up: express trains skip many stations
I should take the regular train
Deciding to take the all-stop train instead — 일반/완행 = the non-express
examples: 이거 급행이에요?
Is this the express?
Ask on the platform before boarding a 1호선 or 9호선 train — yes/no answer tells you whether to wait for the next one.
급행 타면 우리 역 안 서요?
If I take the express, won't it stop at our station?
안 서요 ('doesn't stop') is the danger — the express passes certain stations without stopping.
A: 급행 놓쳤는데 다음 일반 열차 언제 와요? / B: 한 3분이요.
A: I missed the express — when's the next regular train? / B: About 3 minutes.
일반/완행 = all-stop train; the fallback if you miss the express or your station is not an express stop.
nuance: 급행 is Sino-Korean 急行 ('urgent-go' = express), a train or bus service that skips intermediate stations to reach major stops faster. In the Seoul subway, Lines 1, 9, the Gyeongui-Jungang Line, and the Suin-Bundang Line run 급행 trains alongside regular trains on the same tracks. The all-stop alternative is 완행 (緩行, 'slow-go') or, more commonly in everyday speech, 일반 (열차) ('ordinary/regular train'). The must-know verb for stopping is 서다 — '(급행이) 서요?' means 'does the express STOP there?', distinct from '가요?' which asks the destination. You can be on the right line heading the right direction and still overshoot your station if you board the 급행 and your station is not an express stop — this is how 9호선 catches tourists and newcomers. Checking 급행 서요? before boarding is therefore crucial. Signs and platform announcements mark each train as 급행 or 일반; learning to spot the 급행 character on a display board is a worthwhile five-second investment. English speakers who say 빠른 기차 ('fast train') are understood but sound un-natural — the system term is 급행; use it.

structuredNuance.t: 급행(急行) literally 'urgent-go' = an express service that skips intermediate stations. It is faster between major stops but useless if your station is not on the express route. The all-stop alternative is 완행/일반 열차.

Ask on the platform before boarding. Polite -요 with any fellow passenger or station agent. Signs and the digital display above the platform edge show 급행 vs 일반 — watch for this every time you board on 9호선, 1호선, or 경의중앙선.

가요? = does it go (toward) that destination? 서요? = does it stop at that station? On an express, 시청역으로 가요 ('it goes toward City Hall') but 시청역에 안 서요 ('it doesn't stop at City Hall') are both possible if your station is skipped. Always check 서요?, not just 가요?.
급행이에요? → 이거 급행이에요, 일반이에요? (express or regular?), 급행 서요? (does the express stop here?), 급행 안 서요? (doesn't it stop?), 다음 급행 언제 와요? (when's the next express?).

Using 빠른 기차 ('fast train') instead of 급행 sounds unnatural — the system term is 급행. Also, the most common practical mistake is not checking 서요? — an express goes in the right direction but may not stop at your station.

mistakes: Boarding a 급행 without checking it stops at your station.
An express skips many stops. Always confirm 급행 (우리) 역 서요? before boarding, or you will sail past your station. If unsure, take the 일반/완행 (all-stop) train.
Using 가다 instead of 서다 to ask about stopping.
급행 시청역 가요? asks the destination/direction; to ask whether it STOPS there, use 서다: 급행 시청역 서요? The express may 'go' that direction without 'stopping' at your station.
Calling it 빠른 기차 instead of 급행.
빠른 기차 ('fast train') is understandable but not the system term. The correct label is 급행 (express) vs 일반/완행 (all-stop). Use 이거 급행이에요? to ask.

usage: Polite; asking a passenger near the button to press it for you
Checking that the stop has been requested before the bus passes
You press the (alighting) bell to get off
하차벨 = the formal compound; explaining the system to someone who doesn't know
I'll get off next, I'll press the bell
Announcing your intention — 누를게요 (-ㄹ게요) = I'll press it
examples: 벨 눌러 주세요!
Please press the bell!
Said to a passenger standing near the button when you cannot reach it — instinctive, understood immediately.
내릴 거면 미리 벨 눌러요.
If you're getting off, press the bell ahead of time.
미리 ('in advance') is the key word — press the bell before the stop, not exactly at it, so the driver has time to pull over.
A: 벨 안 누르면 그냥 지나가요? / B: 네, 아무도 기다리지 않으면 그냥 가요.
A: If no one presses the bell, does it just drive past? / B: Yes, if no one is waiting there it just goes.
Confirming the most important practical rule: Korean buses skip stops with neither a bell nor a waiting rider.
nuance: 벨 is the loanword 'bell' — in the bus context it always refers to the stop-request button (하차벨, 하차 'alighting' + 벨), and 벨 눌러 주세요 = 'please press the bell', using 누르다 ('to press a button/switch') + the favor form 주세요. The single most important practical fact: Korean city buses do NOT stop at every stop automatically. If no one has pressed the 하차벨 AND no one is standing waiting at the stop, the driver drives right past. So you must press the bell in advance (미리) when your stop is approaching — ideally as the previous stop is passing. The verb is 누르다 (르-irregular: 눌러요/눌러 주세요/눌렀어요); do NOT use 찍다 (that's for tapping the transit card) or 치다 ('to hit/strike') — those are wrong for pressing a button. The formal compound term is 하차벨, but in speech simply 벨 눌러 주세요 or 벨 누르세요 is understood by everyone. If you cannot reach the button on a crowded bus, ask the nearest passenger 벨 좀 눌러 주세요. Subways stop at every station automatically — there is no 벨 underground. Between friends: 벨 눌러 (반말). With the driver or strangers: 벨 눌러 주세요 or 벨 누르세요.

structuredNuance.t: 하차벨 ('alighting bell') = the stop-request button on a Korean city bus. Pressing it signals the driver you want to exit at the next stop. Without a press (and no one waiting outside), the bus drives past.

Bus-only — subways stop at every station automatically. On a bus, press 미리 ('in advance') as the previous stop passes. If you cannot reach the button, ask a neighbor: 벨 좀 눌러 주세요. With strangers: polite -요; with a friend: 벨 눌러 (반말).

누르다 = to press a button/switch — the correct verb for the 벨. 찍다 = to tap/stamp — the correct verb for tapping the transit card on the reader. 치다 = to hit/strike — wrong for either. Do not mix these three verbs.
벨 눌러 주세요 → 하차벨 눌러 주세요 (more formal), 벨 누르세요 (polite imperative without 주세요), 벨 눌렀어요? (did you press?), 벨 누를게요 (I'll press it). The 르-irregular of 누르다: 눌러요, 눌러 주세요, 눌렀어요.

Two traps: (1) assuming the bus stops automatically at every stop — it does NOT; and (2) saying 버튼 ('button') instead of 벨 — 버튼 is understood but 벨 is the idiomatic word for the bus stop-request in Korean.

mistakes: Assuming the bus stops at every stop without pressing the bell.
Korean buses skip a stop if no one pressed the 하차벨 and no one is waiting outside. To exit, press the bell in advance (미리) before your stop arrives, or the bus drives straight past.
Using 찍다 or 치다 for pressing the bell.
찍다 is for tapping the transit card; 치다 means 'to hit/strike'. Pressing a button is 누르다: 벨 눌러 주세요. These verbs are not interchangeable.
Pressing the bell too late, right as the stop arrives.
Press 미리 ('ahead of time') as the previous stop passes — the driver needs enough warning to pull over safely. Pressing at the last second may result in overshooting your stop.
